components.gap: Not covered on the input route. Merin's definitions, distinctions and argument are reconstructed only in part (Merin 2021, pp. 265-274): (a) Definition 8(a), Transparency, also requires the value range of a relevance measure to be a subinterval, proper or improper, of the extended reals; the route states only joint-table dependence and differentiability (rationality-4-3.tex lines 172-180; w02b-p15-024.tex lines 87-90) and never this requirement; (b) Definition 9 adds that ordinal equivalence holds exactly when some strictly increasing (isotonic, n. 9) f gives T = f(T'), and that ordinally equivalent measures can still differ in convenience of range and in algebraic properties; the route states only that fixed increasing transforms preserve rankings (rationality-4-3.tex lines 291-293), not the converse; (c) the argument for the directed notation that, for mutually relevant A and B, A may be more strongly relevant to B than B to A under one measure, less under another and equally under a third (p. 268): the route exhibits only D (asymmetric) and Q (equal) and no measure with the reverse inequality (rationality-4-3.tex lines 235-245, 259-266); (d) the general counterexample to transitivity (p. 266): from A expos B, C expos B and P(AC) = 0 follow A pos B and B pos C by symmetry and A exneg C, hence A neg C; the route gives only one three-outcome instance (lines 75-86); (e) the account of the negation, conjunction and disjunction rules as conditional operation homomorphisms (p. 272): structure-preserving maps from Boolean operations to inversion, addition and weighted mean, essential to predictability of many ordinal and all quantitative relevance properties of logical complexes; every relevance measure affords some homomorphisms under suitably narrow constraints, most of them practically useless, and not every homomorphism is desirable; (f) the raven paradox as Merin states it (pp. 271-272): H supported by A = A1A2, the equivalent G supported by B = B1B2, G supported by C (a white shoe), and the problem that a plausible deductivist criterion treating logical equivalents alike makes B, and with mild further assumptions C, support H, which is counterintuitive; with Merin's account that the unsurprisingness of B makes for its low relevance and that this explains the pretheoretical intuition that B, and C in the augmented story, is irrelevant to H; the route gives only the two support claims and the resolution (rationality-4-3.tex lines 398-425); (g) the informal motivation of section 1 (p. 265): the same relations hold between statements about past events and between possible experimental results and timeless hypotheses, in juristic and scientific diction speaking for B is being evidence for B, and the plausible idea remains vague and prone to apparent exceptions, so a framework is needed; (h) Theorem 10(a) for D and Q is stated only for a nondegenerate target (rationality-4-3.tex lines 440-442), whereas Merin's statement covers every P with P(AB) = 0, degenerate targets included through the neutral completions. Text for most of these exists only in the unrouted handbook/parts/p15/inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02c-p15-027.tex; no file on the handbook input route (handbook/main.tex -> parts/p15.tex, annex/p15.tex) inputs it, so it is not credited.

components.gap: Not covered on the input route. Merin's actual examples, the assumptions limiting them, and the kinds of his claims are presented only in part (Merin 2021, pp. 265-275): (a) the Linda example as given (p. 273): the conjunction fallacy arose most famously in this late-1970s example; E was designed to be representative of F and unrepresentative of B; a surprisingly large proportion of respondents ranked BF above B, contravening P(BF|E) <= P(B|E); many probabilists would explicate the representativeness of a property by the relevance of 'Linda is ...' to the description E, F positive and B negative; the route describes the task and a stipulated model (rationality-4-3.tex lines 479-500) but not the reported result, its date, the representativeness explication, or the standing of that report (no original study cited; no population, design, counts or uncertainty); (b) the empirical and descriptive claims beyond the three that the claim-kind convention says the chapter contains (w02b-p15-024.tex lines 51-59): that there is evidence that delta-p explicates participants' assessments of the relevance of E for H (Skovgaard-Olsen, Singmann & Klauer 2016b) and that the 2016a paper investigated its relation to indicative conditionals (the route only names the research, lines 513-515); that relevance theory, popular in linguistics, conjectures relevance maximization as a general principle of cognition and communication; that LL is widely used in statistics (p. 270); that D, Q and L are the oldest and most commonly used measures (p. 269); that intuitions on amount symmetry are strong only for asymmetric extreme positivity and many will balk at Q's symmetry in the divisibility example (p. 272); that extreme valuation pleases anyone for whom conclusive argument is the strongest argument (p. 272); none is presented and classified with its standing; (c) the drug-and-cure example under the assumptions Merin states (p. 267): propositions about a randomly sampled individual whose credal probabilities reflect statistical frequencies, a drug actually inefficacious, and administration and spontaneous-remission rates both higher among British citizens (the route gives numbers only, lines 118-127); and the qualification that an indicative conditional can also be asserted with less than certainty (p. 266); (d) the raven example's items (1)-(3) with note 15 ('(3) is an inessential embellishment that makes things vivid') and the counterintuitive conclusion it draws (see C02 (f)), and the direction example under three measures (see C02 (c)); (e) the historical claims that the task-relative ordinal results and the disjunctive-evidence results are Merin's own two extensions of the state of the art (Summary, p. 265; 'I offer the following results', p. 271), and the chapter's editorial note that Merin died on 24 May 2019 shortly after finishing it and that the editors made the final minor revisions (p. 274), which bears on attributing the text to Merin. Text for most of these exists only in the unrouted handbook/parts/p15/inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02c-p15-027.tex; no file on the handbook input route (handbook/main.tex -> parts/p15.tex, annex/p15.tex) inputs it, so it is not credited.

components.gap: Not covered on the input route. Not every promised proof or evidence claim of the selected extent is accounted for (Merin 2021, pp. 268-274): (a) Definition 9's claim that ordinal equivalence is equivalent to the existence of an isotonic f with T = f(T') is neither stated nor proved in the direction from ordinal equivalence to f; (b) the stated value ranges of D, Q, L, QL, LL, KO and Z (rationality-4-3.tex lines 248-251) are supported only by bounds and endpoint remarks (annex rationality-4-3.tex lines 102-107); that every value of each stated interval is attained, and so that each listed measure meets Definition 8(a)'s interval requirement, is not shown; (c) the existence claim that every relevance measure affords some homomorphism under suitably narrow constraints (p. 272) is not stated, proved or given a standing; (d) the claim that one measure can make A more relevant to B than B to A, another less, and a third equally (p. 268) is not realized by a model; (e) the empirical report in the Linda example (a surprisingly large proportion of respondents ranked BF above B; late-1970s origin; no study cited by Merin) is given no standing: the proof boundary (w02b-p15-024.tex lines 947-1032) accounts for the cited works but not this reported finding. Text for (a)-(e) exists only in the unrouted handbook/parts/p15/inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02c-p15-027.tex; no file on the handbook input route (handbook/main.tex -> parts/p15.tex, annex/p15.tex) inputs it, so it is not credited.
